name: Liten AI
tagline: A small AI assistant app: chat with a model, keep the useful bits, get on with your day.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Products in this shape are a thin, well-dressed layer over a model API: a chat surface, a place to store what came out of it, and some prompt scaffolding so you do not have to retype your own instructions every morning. A coding agent will get you a local version of that loop in a single session, and it will feel eerily close on day one. The gap is everything around the loop: a mobile client, sync between devices, file and image handling, streaming that does not stutter, and the hundred small interaction decisions that make an assistant feel calm instead of janky. You also inherit the API bill and the maintenance, which is fine until a model deprecation quietly breaks your Saturday. Call it a weekend build with a desktop-only asterisk.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that streams chat from an OpenAI-compatible API, saves every thread and saved snippet to SQLite, and lets you run reusable prompt presets over pasted text.
requirements: An API key for an OpenAI-compatible model provider, in .env
Willingness to pay per token instead of per month
whatYouLose: Mobile and tablet apps, which is where most people actually use an assistant
Cross-device sync without you building or renting a backend
File, PDF and image input handling done properly rather than half done
Whoever is quietly swapping in better models and fixing prompts on your behalf
Any polish in the empty states, keyboard flow and error handling that makes it pleasant
moatNotes: There is no data moat here worth the name. The defensibility is interaction design plus the inertia of your saved history living in their app.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the annoying part of an AI assistant was never the API call. It is having the thing available on your phone at the moment you need it, with your history intact, without you thinking about keys, rate limits or which model got deprecated last week. A subscription is a small price for never being the on-call engineer for your own note-taking. People who build the local version tend to love it for three weeks and then reach for their phone.
notes: Every one of these apps is one model deprecation away from a bad afternoon, hosted or self-built.
prompt:
Build a local-first AI assistant web app called "Smallish". Single repo, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript for the frontend
- Node 20 + Express + better-sqlite3 for the backend, single server file
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- SQLite file at ./data/smallish.db, created on first run
- Model access via any OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint

Secrets: read OPENAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_BASE_URL from .env. Ship a .env.example. Never hardcode a key, never send anything anywhere except the configured endpoint.

Features in scope:
1. Threads: create, rename, delete, list newest first. Messages persist to SQLite.
2. Streaming responses via server-sent events, rendered as markdown with fenced code blocks and a copy button.
3. Presets: named reusable system prompts stored in the DB (e.g. "summarize", "rewrite tighter", "explain this error"). Running a preset on pasted text starts a new thread.
4. Snippets: a keep button on any assistant message that saves it to a snippets table with the source thread id and a timestamp.
5. Search: SQLite FTS5 over messages and snippets, one search box, results jump to the message.
6. Keyboard: cmd+k opens a command palette for new thread, run preset, search. cmd+enter sends.
7. Model picker reading a list from .env, defaulting to the first entry.

Explicitly out of scope: auth, multi-user, mobile app, file uploads, image generation, RAG over a document store, sharing links, any hosted deployment.

Requirements: npm install then npm run dev starts backend and frontend together. Handle a missing key and a failed API call with a visible inline error, not a silent spinner. Include a 20-line README covering setup, where the DB lives, and how to back it up by copying one file.
